1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: A 61-year-old male patient presented to our hospital on Day +34, with the chief complaint of "fever, cough, and chest pain for more than 1 year." Since mid-approximately 13 months before Day 0, he had developed a dry cough, right-sided chest pain described as persistent dull pain, and intermittent fever without obvious cause, with a maximum temperature of 38.5℃, but no chills, rigors, night sweats, fatigue, hemoptysis, or dyspnea. WBC 13.9×10^9/L; chest CT (Day -29): irregular soft-tissue opacity in the right lower lobe, 1 cm in diameter, with no mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Bronchoscopy showed no abnormalities. The remaining examinations were (-); from Day -28 to Day +17, the patient received intermittent anti-infective treatment, with no improvement in symptoms or imaging findings; on Day -348, repeat chest CT showed that the lesion had slightly increased in extent compared with before, with irregular enhancement. On Day -334, thoracoscopic wedge resection of the right lower lobe was performed. Intraoperatively, a mass was seen in the right lower lung near the interlobar fissure, and pathology suggested an inflammatory lesion. The discharge diagnosis was: organizing pneumonia of the right lower lung. In mid-approximately 2 months before Day 0, the patient again developed left-sided chest and back pain, numbness of the lower extremities, sensory disturbance, and limb weakness. There was no cough, sputum production, or fever. Chest CT showed a new nodular lesion in the left lower lobe with peripheral enhancement and enlargement of the left hilar lymph nodes. Postoperative changes were seen in the right lower lobe; MRI: patchy abnormal signal was seen in the T3-T9 vertebral bodies and a compression fracture of the T12 vertebral body, with spinal cord edema, metastasis considered possible. Lung needle biopsy pathology: inflammatory changes with multinucleated giant cells; acid-fast stain negative; bronchoscopy showed no abnormalities; from Day -6 to Day 0, the patient was admitted to the spinal surgery department of our hospital for "low back pain and numbness in both lower extremities" and was diagnosed with "destruction of spinal bone, metastatic tumor?" On Day +5, thoracoscopic resection of the left lower lobe nodule was performed. Pathology suggested: chronic inflammation, organizing pneumonia, and anthracotic pigment deposition; please correlate clinically; pathology slide consultation at a local hospital: chronic interstitial and organizing pneumonia with marked fibrous tissue hyperplasia and collagenization, mild alveolar epithelial hyperplasia, showing inflammatory pseudotumor-like changes. Postoperatively, the patient developed recurrent daily high fever, with temperature up to 39.4℃, and chest pain and cough were markedly worse than before, with a small amount of yellow sputum. WBC 27.9×10^9/L; blood culture and sputum culture were both negative. Anti-infective treatment was ineffective. Repeat chest CT on Day +31 showed that the hilar lesion had enlarged significantly compared with before, and bone destruction of the inferior angle of the left scapula and the glenoid was significantly worse than before. For further diagnosis and treatment, he was admitted to our department. Past medical history, personal history, marital and reproductive history, and family history were unremarkable. On admission, we first performed a physical examination: temperature 37.6℃, chronically ill appearance, pale appearance, multiple enlarged left supraclavicular lymph nodes, hard, immobile, non-tender, with no redness or swelling of the overlying skin; a few moist rales were heard in the left lower lung; cardiac examination (-); abdomen flat; liver palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, slightly firm, with a smooth edge; spleen not palpable; tenderness over the spinous processes of the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae; no edema of the lower extremities. Laboratory examination showed: CBC: WBC 28.0×10^9/L, RBC 2.79×10^12/L, Hb 77 g/L, PLT 232×10^9/L, neutrophil count 23.3×10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 83.3%, lymphocyte percentage 7.4%. Urinalysis was normal, stool routine was normal, OB negative. Liver function showed ALB 23.9 g/L, GLO 35 g/L; renal function, myocardial enzymes, electrolytes, coagulation studies, and D-dimer were normal. Five lung cancer markers were normal. PCT 0.43 μg/L, CRP 94 mg/L↑, ESR 120 mm/h, HIV negative. T-SPOT positive (A: 24, B: 32). PPD skin test (++). Rheumatologic immune lupus panel, ANA profile, and vasculitis testing were negative.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary lung cancer with lymph node and bone metastases
supporting_evidence: A 61-year-old man with pulmonary lesions persisting for more than 1 year, with an irregular soft-tissue opacity in the right lower lung and a newly developed nodular lesion in the left lower lung appearing sequentially, and progressive enlargement of the lesions.
Chest CT showed that the lesion had irregular enhancement and rim enhancement, with imaging features of a space-occupying lesion.

In approximately 2 months before Day 0, left hilar lymphadenopathy developed; on admission physical examination, multiple hard, fixed enlarged lymph nodes were noted in the left supraclavicular region.
MRI showed patchy abnormal signal in the T3-T9 vertebral bodies, a compression fracture of the T12 vertebral body with spinal cord edema; metastasis was considered possible.

Repeat CT on Day +31 showed that the hilar lesion was significantly enlarged compared with the prior study, and bony destruction of the inferior angle of the left scapula and the glenoid was significantly more pronounced than before, suggesting tumor progression and bone involvement
The patient has an anemic appearance, Hb 77 g/L, ALB 23.9 g/L, with manifestations of chronic wasting.
opposing_evidence: Two lung pathology examinations respectively suggested inflammatory lesion/chronic inflammation, organizing pneumonia, and inflammatory pseudotumor-like changes, without direct confirmation of malignancy.
No abnormalities were seen on either of the two bronchoscopic examinations

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis with skeletal tuberculosis/disseminated tuberculosis
supporting_evidence: Prolonged disease course, recurrent fever, cough, and chest pain, with poor response to anti-infective therapy
T-SPOT positive (A: 24, B: 32), PPD skin test (++)
Pathology from lung needle biopsy showed inflammatory changes and multinucleated giant cells, which can be seen in the background of granulomatous lesions
Pulmonary lesions may present as nodules/masses with hilar lymphadenopathy
Spinal bone destruction, abnormal vertebral body signal, and compression fracture can be differentiated from bone tuberculosis
ESR 120 mm/h and CRP 94 mg/L were markedly elevated, suggesting an active inflammatory process
opposing_evidence: The patient had no night sweats or fatigue, and there was no obvious hilar or mediastinal lymphadenopathy in the early stage; direct etiologic evidence of TB was lacking in the first-stage data.

The postoperative pulmonary pathology from both surgeries was mainly described as organizing pneumonia/chronic inflammation, with no clear report of caseous necrosis or typical tuberculous granulomas.

differential_diagnoses.name: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor/inflammatory pseudotumor
supporting_evidence: Pathology slide consultation at the local hospital suggested "chronic interstitial and organizing pneumonia with marked fibrous tissue proliferation and collagenization, mild alveolar epithelial hyperplasia, showing inflammatory pseudotumor-like changes"
Both lung pathology examinations predominantly showed chronic inflammation and organizing pneumonia, with no definite evidence of malignancy.
On imaging, it appears as intrapulmonary nodular/mass-like lesions and may show enhancement, consistent with the characteristic space-occupying appearance of inflammatory pseudotumor.
The patient has fever, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated CRP and ESR, supporting a marked inflammatory response.
opposing_evidence: The presence of osseous destruction of the spine, inferior angle of the scapula, and glenoid, as well as spinal cord edema, should raise greater concern for a malignant or infectious systemic disease and is atypical for a simple pulmonary inflammatory pseudotumor.
Multiple enlarged hard, immobile lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular region are not well explained by a simple benign inflammatory pseudotumor.
Lesions appeared sequentially in both lungs and progressively enlarged, with an extent beyond the usual presentation of a single focal benign inflammatory mass.

differential_diagnoses.name: Organizing pneumonia (including cryptogenic or secondary)
supporting_evidence: In 2015, pathology after wedge resection of the right lower lung indicated an inflammatory lesion, and the discharge diagnosis was organizing pneumonia of the right lower lung.
In 2016, pathology from resection of a left lower lung nodule again indicated "chronic inflammation, with organizing pneumonia identified"
The consultation pathology also described chronic interstitial and organizing pneumonia with fibrous tissue proliferation and collagenization
The patient may have cough, fever, chest pain, and elevated inflammatory markers, consistent with some of the clinical manifestations of organizing pneumonia.
opposing_evidence: The lesions are nodular/mass-like and show enhancement, and the hilar lesion is significantly enlarged, with enlargement of the left hilar and left supraclavicular lymph nodes, more suggestive of a neoplastic lesion or a specific infectious lesion.
There is bony destruction of the spine, scapula, and glenoid; organizing pneumonia alone is difficult to explain.
Long-term anti-infective therapy was ineffective, and the lesions successively appeared and progressed in different lung lobes

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary fungal infection (such as chronic granulomatous mycosis due to Aspergillus and other fungi) with bone involvement
supporting_evidence: Persistent pulmonary lesions without resolution, recurrent fever, anti-infective treatment ineffective
Lung biopsy showed multinucleated giant cells, suggesting possible granulomatous inflammation; fungal infection needs to be differentiated
Imaging shows nodular/mass-like lesions with enhancement, which may resemble chronic fungal infection
WBC was markedly elevated, and CRP and ESR were significantly elevated, suggesting a persistent inflammatory response.
opposing_evidence: The phase I information did not provide positive mycological examination evidence.
HIV negative; the first stage did not indicate a definite immunosuppressive background.
Pathology did not describe characteristic findings such as fungal hyphae or spores.

differential_diagnoses.name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis or other systemic noninfectious granulomatous disease
supporting_evidence: Pulmonary nodular/mass-like lesions; pathology shows chronic inflammation and multinucleated giant cells, which can be differentiated from noninfectious granulomatous diseases
A systemic inflammatory response may occur, with fever and markedly elevated ESR and CRP.
Complex manifestations with multisite involvement; coexisting pulmonary and bone/spinal lesions suggest the possibility of a systemic disease
opposing_evidence: Rheumatologic/immunologic testing for lupus, ANA panel, and vasculitis was negative
In the first stage, there was no evidence of typical systemic vasculitis such as upper airway or renal involvement, and urinalysis was normal.

Imaging and clinical findings more prominently indicate a space-occupying hilar lesion, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and bone destruction; malignancy or TB should be prioritized for consideration.

recommended_exams.exam: Blood tests (CBC, CRP, ESR, liver and kidney function, albumin/globulin, PCT, T-SPOT, PPD, HIV, rheumatologic autoantibody panel)
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the whole spine
Abdominal color Doppler ultrasound (liver, spleen, abdominal lymph nodes)

stage2_input.text: After admission, the patient underwent further examinations: Color Doppler ultrasound: hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and multiple nodules within the spleen. Multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the abdominal cavity and retroperitoneum. Multiple enlarged left supraclavicular lymph nodes and a fluid-containing mass in the left neck. Lung CT (Day +36): left hilar mass, lung cancer highly suspected, with enlargement of mediastinal, bilateral hilar, supraclavicular fossa, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes. Bone destruction of the bilateral sternum, clavicles, first ribs, and multiple vertebrae at T2, T6, and T12. Postoperative changes in the right middle lung and left lower lung. MRI (Day +36): Findings: multiple patchy long T1 and T2 signal lesions of varying sizes were seen within the vertebral bodies and spinous processes of T1-T12 and L1, L2, L5, and S1, with marked enhancement after contrast administration. The T12 vertebral body was markedly compressed and flattened, with obvious posterior compression and narrowing of the spinal canal, and marked compression of the spinal cord at the corresponding level. Impression: multiple osseous destructive lesions involving the thoracic and lumbar vertebral bodies and posterior elements, metastases highly suspected; please correlate clinically. Compression and flattening of the T12 vertebral body. Bronchoscopy (Day +38): at the inferior opening of the left upper lobe, the left lower lobe, and the lower segment of the left main bronchus, numerous nodular protrusions were seen, with an uneven surface; the tissue was soft on forceps biopsy and bled easily. Diagnosis: left bronchial lesion, cancer? Pathology result: chronic mucosal inflammation, PAS (-), acid-fast (-). Summary of the patient's features: elderly man, chronic course, prolonged fever, cough, pulmonary nodules, hepatosplenomegaly, generalized superficial and deep lymphadenopathy, and osseous destruction. recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had a disease course of more than 1 year, with persistent fever, cough, and chest pain. Imaging showed a left hilar mass with progressive enlargement, accompanied by enlarged mediastinal, bilateral hilar, supraclavicular fossa, and retroperitoneal lymph nodes, as well as multiple areas of bone destruction. Clinically, in addition to metastatic lung cancer, chronic infections such as TB, nontuberculous mycobacteria, and fungal infection should also be considered. Two previous bronchoscopies were either unremarkable or showed only chronic inflammation, but the hilar and peribronchial lesions continued to progress. Repeat bronchoscopy was performed to directly reassess whether there were newly developed nodular, infiltrative, or friable lesions within the airway, to identify a more representative site for sampling, and to obtain secretions or tissue for pathology and etiologic testing. This examination helps explain the relationship between the hilar mass and the bronchial lesions, distinguish neoplastic lesions from granulomatous infection, and provide a basis for whether to continue invasive sampling and for the direction of anti-infective treatment.

The patient had prolonged fever, was unresponsive to routine anti-infective therapy, and had a positive T-SPOT. Coexisting pulmonary nodules/masses, extensive lymphadenopathy, liver and spleen involvement with splenic nodules, and bone destruction were present. Repeated pathology showed only chronic inflammation and multinucleated giant cells, suggesting that mycobacterial infection remained an important differential diagnosis. Acid-fast staining was repeated on specimens obtained by follow-up bronchoscopy with the aim of directly identifying evidence of acid-fast bacilli at the site of the pulmonary primary lesion or active respiratory tract involvement, to help distinguish common bacterial infection, fungal infection, tumor, and mycobacterial infection. Although the result was negative, this test still had important exclusionary value: on the one hand, it indicates that the bacterial load in the respiratory specimen may have been low and that the sensitivity of a single smear is limited, so mycobacterial disease cannot be excluded on this basis; on the other hand, it prompted the clinical team to continue searching for extrapulmonary lesion specimens with a higher positive yield.

Postoperatively, the patient had recurrent high fever up to 39.4℃, a marked elevation in the white blood cell count, and significantly increased CRP and ESR, along with worsening cough and scant yellow sputum, indicating obvious infectious inflammation. However, repeated conventional anti-infective treatment was ineffective; therefore, bacterial and fungal cultures of bronchoscopy-related specimens were needed to evaluate for chronic suppurative bacterial infection and disseminated fungal infection. In the previous differential diagnosis, Nocardia, Actinomyces, Cryptococcus, and Talaromyces marneffei had been considered. Negative cultures would help reduce the likelihood of ordinary bacterial infection and common fungal infection as the primary cause, and further shift the diagnostic focus toward special pathogens such as mycobacteria. This testing is meaningful for avoiding blindly escalating conventional antibacterial or antifungal treatment and reducing the risk of unnecessary medication use in subsequent management.

recommended_exams.exam: Puncture of left supraclavicular cystic mass
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Needle aspiration of the left supraclavicular fluid-filled mass yielded approximately 5 mL of purulent secretions
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: On admission physical examination, multiple enlarged left supraclavicular lymph nodes had already been identified. Imaging suggested a fluid-containing mass in the left neck. The patient also had generalized superficial and deep lymphadenopathy, prolonged fever, and a wasting state. Previous multiple pulmonary tissue samplings had not established the etiology, whereas a superficial fluid-containing lesion was more accessible, carried lower risk, and often had a higher positive yield. Needle aspiration of the left supraclavicular fluid-containing mass was performed, on the one hand, to determine whether its nature was a necrotic liquefied lymph node, an abscess, or tumor necrosis; on the other hand, it could directly obtain purulent secretions for acid-fast staining, culture, and cytology/pathologic examination when necessary. This examination could seek etiologic evidence from a more representative extrapulmonary lesion and played a निर्णing role in making the key distinction among malignancy, TB, nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, and fungal infection.

Immediately sending the purulent secretion obtained by aspiration of the left supraclavicular fluid collection for acid-fast staining was because the patient's systemic manifestations were highly suggestive of a chronic granulomatous or mycobacterial disease: prolonged disease course, recurrent high fever, ineffective antibacterial therapy, mass-like pulmonary lesions, generalized lymphadenopathy, liver and spleen involvement, and multiple osseous destructive lesions, with prior lung tissue pathology showing multinucleated giant cells and a background of chronic inflammation. Performing acid-fast staining on the purulent specimen can rapidly provide direct evidence of whether acid-fast bacilli are present; compared with repeatedly obtaining samples from pulmonary lesions, fluid from a superficial abscess is often more likely to yield the pathogen. A positive result markedly shifted the clinical consideration from “tumor or nonspecific inflammation” toward mycobacterial infection, and also provided a key basis for the required subsequent species culture and identification, differentiation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria, and formulation of a targeted treatment plan.

A positive acid-fast stain can only indicate the presence of acid-fast bacilli and cannot distinguish Mycobacterium tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria, and throughout the entire course of this case, TB and nontuberculous mycobacteria were always important differential diagnoses. Although the patient had a positive T-SPOT and PPD (++), the imaging findings were dominated by a mass-like lesion in the middle and lower lungs, extensive lymphadenopathy, hepatic and splenic nodules including intrasplenic nodules, and multiple destructive bone lesions throughout the body; prior pathology also lacked typical caseous necrosis, suggesting that simple TB was not entirely consistent. The purpose of performing mycobacterial culture on the aspirated pus was to obtain etiologic confirmation and species identification, to determine whether the infection was due to TB or nontuberculous mycobacteria. The culture result was Mycobacterium avium, which directly determined the final diagnosis as disseminated Mycobacterium avium disease and influenced the subsequent choice of treatment regimen, avoiding management according to the standard TB regimen by mistake.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Left supraclavicular abscess debridement, pathology showed chronic granulomatous inflammation
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although acid-fast staining and culture of the aspirated fluid can provide etiologic evidence, the patient’s systemic imaging findings were highly similar to advanced malignant tumor, and multiple prior lung pathology examinations consistently showed no cancer cells; therefore, pathologic examination of the specimen from left supraclavicular abscess debridement was still required to determine the nature of the lesion at the tissue level. Pathology can assess for the presence of chronic granulomatous inflammation, necrosis, suppurative changes, or tumor components, thereby making an important distinction between infectious granuloma and metastatic malignant tumor. In this case, pathology showing chronic granulomatous inflammation, together with positive acid-fast staining of the pus and subsequent culture identifying Mycobacterium avium, mutually corroborated each other, supporting the histologic basis for mycobacterial infection and also helping to exclude previously highly suspected diseases such as metastatic lung cancer and lymphoma, thus providing the basis for the final diagnosis and implementation of combination therapy targeting nontuberculous mycobacteria.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Repeat bronchoscopy was performed; repeat acid-fast staining was (-), and bacterial and fungal cultures were (-). Aspiration of the left supraclavicular fluid-filled mass yielded approximately 5 ml of purulent secretions, which were sent for acid-fast staining (+); mycobacterial culture grew Mycobacterium avium. Left supraclavicular abscess debridement was performed, and pathology showed chronic granulomatous inflammation.

2. Physical examination: Temperature 37.6℃, chronically ill appearance, anemic appearance, multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular region, hepatomegaly, spinous process tenderness.

3. Ancillary examinations: abnormally elevated white blood cell count, anemia, T-SPOT positive, a pulmonary space-occupying lesion, multiple bone destruction lesions, hepatosplenomegaly, multiple splenic nodules, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Repeated lung tissue biopsies on pathology showed chronic inflammation. Multinucleated giant cells were also seen. Lymph node biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation.
